D. Fish and Shellfish Comments and FDA Response

Salt is a required or optional ingredient in several SOI in part 161 (21 CFR part 161) Fish and shellfish. We proposed amending the following SOI in part 161 which permit salt as a required or optional ingredient: Canned oysters (Sec. 161.145), Canned Pacific salmon (Sec. 161.170), Canned wet pack shrimp in transparent or nontransparent containers (Sec. 161.173), and Canned tuna (Sec. 161.190). We did not propose to amend the SOI for Oysters (Sec. 161.130), Frozen raw breaded shrimp (Sec. 161.175), and Frozen raw lightly breaded shrimp (Sec. 161.176). The SOI for oysters (Sec. 161.130) does not include salt as a required or optional ingredient. Instead, the SOI provides for the optional use of saltwater containing less than 0.75 percent salt in the shucking of oysters (Sec. 161.130(b)). In the proposed rule, we described our understanding that current industry practice is to use accessible seawater rather than to constitute a solution for the shucking process. Therefore, because salt was not an added ingredient, we did not propose to amend the SOI to allow salt substitutes. We requested comment on this approach and our understanding of current industry practice (see 88 FR 21148 at 21152). (Comment 18) One comment asks us to amend the SOI for oysters (Sec. 161.130) to allow for the use of salt substitutes. The comment acknowledges that current industry practice is not to use a prepared salt and water solution for the processing of oysters but suggests that we permit the use of salt substitutes in the SOI for oysters to accommodate any future use of salt substitutes in such solution. (Response 18) The SOI for oysters prescribes the amount of salt present in the saltwater solution (less than 0.75 percent salt) and the length of time the oysters are in contact with the water or saltwater solution (not more than 30 minutes) (see Sec. 161.130(b)). These parameters were set to help ensure that no appreciable loss of solids or absorption of water occurs during washing, which could impact flavor and nutritive content of the oysters (see 11 FR 9331 at 9332-9333, August 27, 1946). Allowing the use of salt substitutes to lower the salt content of this solution without also changing the other parameters, such as length of time the oysters are in contact with water, could affect the amount of shrinkage or water absorption of the oysters. Further, the SOI requires that the oysters are packed without any added substance (see Sec. 161.130(b)). The effect of using salt substitutes for processing oysters is unlikely to be the same as using salt, which could result in oysters being packed with an added substance. Therefore, we decline to amend the SOI for oysters in the final rule. (Comment 19) One comment requests that the SOI for frozen raw breaded shrimp at Sec. 161.175 and, by reference, the SOI for frozen raw lightly breaded shrimp at Sec. 161.176, also be amended to permit the use of salt substitutes. The comment explains that these SOI allow for safe and suitable batter and breading ingredients but prohibit the use of artificial flavorings, artificial sweeteners, artificial colors, and chemical preservatives. The comment would amend the SOI to explicitly allow salt substitutes and also provide that use of a salt substitute is not limited by the existing ingredient prohibitions in the SOI. (Response 19) As previously discussed, we intended to amend SOI that include salt as a required or optional ingredient to provide manufacturers with ingredient flexibility to reduce salt in these foods. The SOI for frozen raw breaded shrimp at Sec. 161.175 does not explicitly provide for the use of salt as an ingredient. The SOI provides for the use of safe and suitable batter and breading ingredients (Sec. 161.175(a)), but excludes artificial flavorings, artificial sweeteners, artificial colors, and chemical preservatives (Sec. 161.175(d)). Thus, manufacturers can use salt and salt substitutes that are not artificial flavorings, artificial sweeteners, artificial colors, or chemical preservatives in frozen raw breaded shrimp. Therefore, we decline to amend the SOI for frozen raw breaded shrimp (Sec. 161.175) to explicitly permit salt substitutes. Because the SOI for frozen raw lightly breaded shrimp at Sec. 161.176 cross references Sec. 161.175, we are not amending the SOI for frozen raw lightly breaded shrimp for the same reasons.

DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY

U.S. Customs and Border Protection

19 CFR Part 123

[Docket No. USCBP-2026-0992] RIN 1651-AB60

Advance Traveler Information for Rail

AGENCY: U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.

ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking.

SUMMARY: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is proposing to require rail carriers to transmit advance electronic traveler information to CBP for any individual (crew and passengers) who is arriving in or departing from the United States on board a train. The rail carrier also would be required to transmit an advance notice of arrival or departure, as applicable, for the train. This rule would enhance security while facilitating legitimate international travel on board trains.

DATES: Comments must be received by December 14, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Public Participation

Interested persons are invited to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written data, views, or arguments on all aspects of the notice of proposed rulemaking. CBP also invites comments that relate to the economic, environmental, or federalism effects that might result from this proposal. Comments that will provide the most assistance to CBP will reference a specific portion of the proposed rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include data, information, or authority that support such recommended change.

II. Executive Summary

A. Purpose of the Rulemaking

The purpose of this proposed rule is to increase security in the rail environment while simultaneously facilitating the legitimate travel of passengers and crew. The current regulations applicable to rail carriers fail to provide CBP with timely information necessary to evaluate in advance the risk of individuals arriving in or departing from the United States by train; or to detect violations relating to immigration, customs, agricultural, or other laws that CBP is responsible for enforcing or administering. The lack of this advance information in the rail environment has left a gap in U.S. national security that terrorists or other criminals could exploit. This risk has increased for rail travel as security measures for other modes of travel, such as air and commercial vessels, have increased. To respond to this risk, CBP established a program that allows rail carriers to voluntarily transmit to CBP advance electronic information relating to individuals arriving in or departing from the United States on board a train. CBP regularly uses the voluntarily transmitted information to identify rail travelers requiring additional vetting or inspection and to identify violations of immigration, customs, agriculture, and other laws while simultaneously facilitating the travel of legitimate passengers and crew.

Based on this experience with the voluntary program, CBP has determined that the proposed mandatory reporting requirements are necessary to ensure CBP has sufficient and reliable information and the time necessary to perform its border security obligations for all international rail traffic. Mandatory reporting of this information would also ensure that CBP receives accurate and timely information in an acceptable format, which is essential for an effective vetting process. By mandating the transmission of this electronic information in advance, CBP would improve its ability to: (1) vet all travelers attempting to cross the U.S. border on board a train; and (2) timely respond to any identified risk or non-compliance with U.S. civil or criminal laws that CBP enforces or administers. CBP also expects that the knowledge that all rail travelers will be vetted in advance would deter travelers planning to use rail travel for illicit purposes. Additionally, the proposed rule is intended to increase CBP's operational efficiency. Based on CBP's experience with the voluntary program, when the required information is received in advance and the data is accurate and complete, the overall processing time for that train and the travelers on board improves. As a result of increased efficiencies and the additional electronic information received in advance, this rule would enable CBP officers to focus their resources more effectively at ports of entry through improved vetting and targeting. Finally, this proposed rule would promote CBP's efforts to continue to move toward establishing consistent procedures across all modes of transportation and ports of entry.

B. Legal Authority

The requirements proposed by this rule are authorized pursuant to sections 431 and 433 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (Tariff Act) (19 U.S.C. 1431, 1433). Specifically, section 433(d) of the Tariff Act requires the person in charge of a vehicle (which includes a train) to transmit to the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary), pursuant to an electronic data interchange system, such information, data, documents, papers, or manifests that the Secretary may require by regulation. 19 U.S.C. 1433(d). Section 431(b) of the Tariff Act requires that the master, person in charge of a vehicle (including a train), or an authorized agent of the owner or operator of a vehicle, sign, produce, deliver, or electronically transmit any manifest required by the Secretary in accordance with the regulations. 19 U.S.C. 1431(b).

Sections 403(1) and 411 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135, 2178-79), codified at 6 U.S.C. 203(1) and 211, transferred certain functions from the U.S. Customs Service of the Department of the Treasury to the Department of Homeland Security. Sections 431(b) and 433(d) of the Tariff Act (19 U.S.C. 1431(b), 1433(d)) impose requirements on vehicle transportation. The term ``vehicle'' includes ``every description of carriage or other contrivance used, or capable of being used, as a means of transportation on land, but does not include aircraft.'' Tariff Act sec. 401(b) (19 U.S.C. 1401(b)). Accordingly, sections 431(b) and 433(d) of the Tariff Act (19 U.S.C. 1431, 1433) apply to rail transportation.

Section 431(d) of the Tariff Act requires the Secretary to promulgate regulations that specify the form for and the information and data that must be contained in a manifest and prescribe the manner of production for, and the delivery for electronic transmittal of, a manifest. 19 U.S.C. 1431(d). Finally, section 433(e) of the Tariff Act states that a train arriving in the United States may only depart from the port or place of arrival in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary, unless otherwise authorized by law. 19 U.S.C. 1433(e).

C. Summary of the Proposed Rule

This rule would require rail carriers to transmit an advance notice of arrival or departure, as applicable, for any train that is arriving in or departing from the United States with a traveler on board, including a train that crosses the U.S. border while in transit. The notice of arrival and notice of departure would be due no later than 24 hours prior to the train's arrival at the U.S. border crossing location on the inbound and outbound trips, respectively. Additionally, the rule would require rail carriers to transmit advance electronic traveler information to CBP for any individual (including crew and passengers) who will arrive in or depart from the United States on board the train or who crosses the U.S. border while in transit. The required information would include information generally found on a passport or other DHS-approved travel document, including name, date of birth, sex, country of citizenship, country of residence, and DHS-approved travel document type, number, country of issuance and expiration date, if applicable. The information would also include other identifying information such as status on board the train (i.e., conductor, engineer, passenger, crew); complete itinerary of the traveler; address while in the United States for all travelers, except those in transit; alien registration number, if applicable; traveler's passenger name record locator, if available; known traveler number, if applicable; redress number, if applicable; baggage tag information, if applicable; and seat location, including car and seat number, if available. The required information would also include contact phone number with country code and email address, if available. After the rail carrier transmits the required information, CBP would conduct an initial vetting of the advance information and send a response message to the carrier. The response message would state either that CBP accepted the transmission or that the rail carrier must contact CBP prior to departure. If CBP's vetting of the traveler information does not identify any traveler of concern, then the response message will state that CBP has accepted the transmission. In such a case, no further advance action by the rail carrier is required. However, if CBP has identified a traveler of concern, then the response message will indicate that the carrier should call CBP and will provide a phone number for the carrier to call. Upon contacting CBP, the carrier and CBP will attempt to resolve any concerns regarding the traveler, such as by confirming whether there are any errors in the transmitted information. If CBP's vetting flags a traveler as having potential security, immigration, customs, or other law enforcement issues, then CBP may recommend that the carrier not board the traveler. Carriers would have two options for transmitting the required advance electronic information to CBP. Under the first option, rail carriers would transmit the advance electronic information through a CBP-certified transmission system. Under this option, a carrier would be required to submit its electronic transmission system to CBP for testing and CBP would have to certify that the rail carrier's system is capable of communicating with the CBP system for effective transmissions of data and receipt of appropriate messages. Under the second option, rail carriers could transmit the advance electronic information through any CBP-approved electronic data interchange system, such as the Electronic Advance Passenger Information System (eAPIS) web portal, or any CBP-approved application with manifest capabilities.

III. Background and Purpose

A. Legal Authority

These proposed regulations are authorized by sections 431 and 433 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (Tariff Act) (19 U.S.C. 1431, 1433). Specifically, section 433(d) of the Tariff Act requires the person in charge of a vehicle (which includes trains) to transmit to the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary), pursuant to an electronic data interchange system, such information, data, documents, papers, or manifests that the Secretary may require by regulation. 19 U.S.C. 1433(d). Section 431(b) of the Tariff Act requires that the master, person in charge of a vehicle, or an authorized agent of the owner or operator of a vehicle, to sign, produce, deliver, or electronically transmit any manifest required by the Secretary in accordance with the regulations. 19 U.S.C. 1431(b).

Sections 403(1) and 411 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (Pub. L. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135, 2178-79, codified at 6 U.S.C. 203(1) and 211, transferred certain functions from the U.S. Customs Service of the Department of the Treasury to the Department of Homeland Security. Sections 431(b) and 433(d) of the Tariff Act (19 U.S.C. 1431(b), 1433(d)) impose requirements on vehicle transportation. The term ``vehicle'' includes ``every description of carriage or other contrivance used, or capable of being used, as a means of transportation on land, but does not include aircraft.'' Tariff Act sec. 401(b) (19 U.S.C. 1401(b)). Accordingly, sections 431(b) and 433(b) of the Tariff Act (19 U.S.C. 1431, 1433) apply to rail transportation.

Section 431(d) of the Tariff Act requires the Secretary to promulgate regulations that specify the form for and the information and data that must be contained in a manifest and prescribe the manner of production for, and the delivery for electronic transmittal of, a manifest. 19 U.S.C. 1431(d). Additionally, a train arriving in the United States may only depart from the port or place of arrival in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary, unless otherwise authorized by law. Tariff Act sec. 433(e) (19 U.S.C. 1433(e)). These statutory provisions grant the Secretary the authority to issue regulations that require a person in charge of a train to electronically transmit data, documents, papers, or manifests and to specify in the regulations what information and data must be transmitted. The Secretary has delegated its statutory authority relating to these requirements to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP). See DHS, Delegation No. 07010.3, Delegation of Authority to the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection II.A (Rev. No. 03.2, Incorporating Change 2) (Dec. 11, 2024).

B. Current Regulations and Need for Rulemaking

CBP intends for this rulemaking to promote the dual goals of increasing security in the rail environment while simultaneously facilitating the legitimate international travel of passengers and crew. CBP developed these proposed regulations based on its experience with a voluntary program that permits rail carriers to transmit advance electronic traveler information to CBP and the successful implementation of similar regulations for air carriers and commercial vessel carriers. This section discusses the current requirements applicable to rail carriers and the insufficiencies of those requirements. This section also describes the voluntary program for rail carriers and the current regulations for air carriers and commercial vessel carriers. 1. Current Regulations for Rail Carriers Rail carriers operating trains that cross the U.S. border with either Mexico or Canada are subject to part 123 of title 19 of the Code of Federal Regulations (19 CFR part 123). Part 123 includes provisions governing the report of arrival, manifesting, unlading and lading, instruments of international traffic, shipments in transit, commercial traveler's samples, and baggage. Pursuant to 19 CFR part 123, rail carriers are required to make a report of arrival to CBP for any train arriving in the United States from a foreign location. 19 CFR 123.1(b). The report of arrival must be made upon arrival of the train at the U.S. port of entry. 19 CFR 123.1(b). Individuals arriving in the United States from a foreign location on board a train must report their arrival to CBP once they arrive in the United States. 19 CFR 123.1(a). Rail carriers are also subject to reporting requirements relating to baggage, merchandise, and commercial cargo traveling on board a train arriving in the United States from a foreign location. For example, the conductor of a train is required to present to CBP individual car manifests and a train sheet, sometimes called a consist, bridge sheet, or trip sheet, listing each car and showing the car numbers and initials. 19 CFR 123.6. Additionally, baggage or merchandise carried on a train arriving from a foreign location must be listed on an inward foreign manifest and must be presented to a CBP officer at the time the rail carrier makes the report of arrival, unless an exception applies. 19 CFR 123.3 and 123.5. Finally, for any train arriving in the United States from a foreign location with commercial cargo on board, the rail carrier must electronically transmit certain information concerning the cargo to CBP two hours prior to the cargo's arrival at its first U.S. port of entry. 19 CFR 123.91. The required information generally identifies the rail carrier, the shipper, the consignee, and the train; includes a description of the cargo; and specifies when the train will arrive in the United States. See 19 CFR 123.91(d). See 19 CFR part 123, subparts C and D (merchandise), subpart G (baggage), and subpart J (commercial cargo). When baggage arrives in the actual possession of a traveler, the traveler's declaration will be accepted in lieu of a manifest. See 19 CFR 123.3(b) and 123.62. Merchandise transported from one U.S. port to another U.S. port through Canada or Mexico may be included on an in-transit manifest. See 19 CFR part 123, subpart C. Merchandise transported in transit across the United States to Canada or Mexico is governed by 19 CFR part 18. Specifically, the rail carrier must transmit the following information for all required incoming cargo: the rail carrier identification code; the carrier-assigned conveyance name, equipment number and trip number; the scheduled date and time of arrival at the first port of entry in the United States; the numbers and quantities of the cargo laden on board the train; a precise cargo description; the shipper's complete name and address or identification number; the name and address of the consignee; the place where the rail carrier takes possession of the cargo shipment; any hazardous material code; container numbers or rail car numbers; and the seal numbers for all seals affixed to containers and/or rail cars. 19 CFR 123.91(d).

In 2005, CBP established a program that allows rail carriers to voluntarily transmit to CBP manifest information relating to individuals arriving in or departing from the United States on board a train. The purpose of the voluntary program is to respond to the threat in the rail environment and to more effectively identify rail travelers requiring additional vetting or inspection, while facilitating legitimate international travel and trade. This voluntary program requests that rail carriers transmit to CBP information regarding the rail carrier, the train's route, and each individual on board the train. Specifically, CBP requests the following data: rail carrier's name, point of contact, carrier's telephone number and email address, carrier code, trip identifier, departure/arrival location code, and estimated time of departure/arrival. See APIS-VRBS PIA at 2-3. Additionally, CBP requests the following data elements for each individual traveling on board the train: name; date of birth; sex; DHS-approved travel document type, number, and issuing country, if required; traveler status (passenger or crew); address, if available; and departure or arrival code. Id. This information is generally referred to as manifest information or as an arrival or departure manifest. Id. at 1.

CBP regularly uses the voluntarily transmitted information to identify rail travelers requiring additional vetting or inspection and to identify violations of immigration, customs, agriculture, and other laws while simultaneously facilitating the international travel of legitimate passengers and crew. Id. One rail carrier currently voluntarily transmits information to CBP through this voluntary program. Id. However, because the transmission of the information is not mandatory and there are no penalties for noncompliance, the information transmitted is not always complete, valid, timely, or in an electronic format. When the transmitted information is incomplete or inaccurate, CBP officers must update the information when inspecting the train at the U.S. port of entry or may not use the advance information for processing at all. Additionally, not all carriers currently participate in the voluntary program. Making the reporting mandatory, along with the requirement for rail carriers to verify travel documents against transmitted information, will ensure that CBP receives accurate and timely information, which is essential for an effective vetting process. This improved data quality directly contributes to more reliable security assessments. Based on this experience, CBP has determined that the proposed mandatory reporting requirements are necessary to ensure CBP has sufficient and reliable information and the time necessary to perform its border security obligations for all international rail traffic. Mandatory reporting of this information would also ensure that CBP receives accurate and timely information, in an accessible electronic format, which is essential for effective advance vetting processes. By mandating the transmission of this information in advance, CBP would improve its ability to: (1) pre-vet all travelers attempting to cross the U.S. border on board a train; and (2) timely respond to any identified risk or non-compliance with U.S. civil or criminal laws enforced or administered by CBP. This means that if a traveler of concern is identified during vetting, CBP has sufficient time to investigate, resolve concerns, or prepare for an interdiction, rather than reacting in real-time at the border, which can be less efficient and potentially more dangerous. CBP also expects that the knowledge that all rail travelers will be vetted in advance would deter travelers planning to use rail travel for illicit purposes. Accordingly, this proposed rule would support CBP's core missions of border security, including screening, reviewing, identifying, and prioritizing the inspection of travelers arriving in and departing from the United States; detecting, responding to, and interdicting terrorists, drug smugglers and traffickers, human smugglers and traffickers, and other persons who may undermine the security of the United States; and ensuring the interdiction of persons illegally entering the United States. See, e.g., 6 U.S.C. 211(c). Additionally, the proposed rule is intended to increase efficiency in CBP's ability to process individuals arriving in or departing from the United States on board a train. Based on the experience with the voluntary program, when the required information is received in advance and the data is accurate and complete, the overall processing time for that train and the travelers on board improves. With advance information, CBP officers can access the data prior to traveler arrival and use the information to make better informed admissibility and enforcement decisions. By identifying high-risk individuals in advance, CBP officers can focus their resources more effectively at ports of entry. This allows for quicker processing of legitimate travelers while dedicating more attention to those who require additional scrutiny, thereby optimizing security operations. Additionally, by mandating the advance information, CBP would improve the accuracy and completeness of the traveler data so that advance technologies could be used effectively. For example, when CBP has access to advance traveler information, CBP is able to use the Traveler Verification Service to build galleries of photographs based on arriving or departing individuals, which facilitates traveler processing. CBP processes large volumes of travelers at the rail ports of entry every day, and increasing efficiencies for CBP train traveler operations would result in benefits to all entities that are processed by CBP.

Finally, this proposed rule would promote CBP's efforts to continue to move toward establishing consistent procedures across all modes of transportation and ports of entry. The Advance Passenger Information System (APIS) requirements currently in effect for passengers and crew arriving or departing on board aircraft and commercial vessels, described in Section III.B.3. of this document below, have been successful at promoting both security and the international travel of legitimate passengers, and CBP proposes to implement similar requirements for other modes of travel. In addition to this rule, CBP also expects to propose similar reporting requirements for cross-border bus travel. CBP's goal is to ensure a consistent level of security across all modes of cross-border transportation. In conclusion, CBP is proposing mandatory advance reporting requirements for passengers and crew arriving and departing the United States on board a train. CBP would use the information to identify high-risk passengers and crew who may: pose a risk to border or public security; be a terrorist or suspected terrorist or affiliated with or suspected of being affiliated with terrorists or terrorist organizations; be a person of interest; otherwise be engaged in activity in violation of U.S. law; be the subject of wants or warrants; or be inadmissible, while simultaneously facilitating the international travel of legitimate passengers and crew. 3. Current Regulations for Commercial Air Carriers, Private Aircraft and Commercial Vessel Carriers In order to address the concerns identified above in the rail environment, CBP is proposing reporting requirements for rail carriers that are very similar to the regulations currently applicable to air carriers and commercial vessel carriers. Accordingly, a brief summary of those requirements follows.

For regulations relating to commercial aircraft, see 19 CFR 122.49a, 122.49b, 122.49c, 122.75a, and 122.75b. For regulations relating to commercial vessels, see 19 CFR 4.7b and 4.64.

In response to the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, CBP developed regulations requiring commercial air carriers or commercial vessels to electronically transmit prior to departure information relating to individuals traveling to or from the United States on board commercial air carriers or commercial vessels. CBP also developed similar regulations requiring private aircraft pilots to electronically transmit information for individuals travelling on board private aircraft arriving in and departing from the United States. See 19 CFR 122.22.

[CIS No. 2870-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0529] RIN 1615-AD26

Removing Deference to Prior USCIS Determinations of Eligibility

AGENCY: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, DHS.

ACTION: Notice of proposed rulemaking.

SUMMARY: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), proposes to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), which generally provides that USCIS gives deference to a prior approval involving the same facts when adjudicating a request to extend a petition for an alien's employment or stay. This change would better align DHS regulations with the statute, which places the burden of proving eligibility for all immigration benefits on the petitioner, applicant, or beneficiary; strengthen adjudicatory review; and support agency priorities to improve the integrity of the immigration system and better protect the interests of U.S. workers.

I. Public Participation

II. Background

A. Purpose and Summary of the Proposed Regulatory Action

The purpose of this proposed rule is to remove 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5). That regulation instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of a petitioner's, applicant's, or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts. This requirement most often applies when a petitioning employer seeks to extend a petition for an alien's employment or authorized stay in the United States under the same previously approved nonimmigrant worker classification. Under the current regulation, USCIS must generally defer to the prior determination of eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information. 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5).

For most nonimmigrant classifications that use Form I-129, the filer is referred to as the ``petitioner.'' However, for some classifications (for example, the E and TN classifications), the filer is referred to as the ``applicant.'' For simplicity, references in this preamble to a ``petitioner'' also include an ``applicant,'' and references to a ``petition'' also include an ``application.''

B. Legal Authority

The Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary)'s authority for these proposed regulatory amendments is found in various sections of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA), Public Law 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135, 6 U.S.C. 101 et seq. General authority for issuing this proposed rule is found in section 103(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a), which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 112, which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations. Further authority for these proposed regulatory amendments is found in:

Although several provisions of the INA discussed in this NPRM refer exclusively to the ``Attorney General,'' such provisions are now to be read as referring to the Secretary of Homeland Security by operation of the HSA. See 6 U.S.C. 202(3), 251, 271(b), 542 note, 557; 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (g), 1551 note; Nielsen v. Preap, 586 U.S. 392, 397 n.2 (2019).

Section 214(a)(1) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1), which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe, by regulation, the time and conditions of the admission of nonimmigrants; Section 214(c)(1) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(1), which, inter alia, authorizes the Secretary to prescribe how an importing employer may petition for nonimmigrant workers, as well as the form of the petition and the information that an importing employer must provide in the petition; Section 235(d)(3) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1225(d)(3), which authorizes ``any immigration officer . . . to administer oaths and to take and consider evidence of or from any person touching the privilege of any alien or person he believes or suspects to be an alien to enter, reenter, transit through, or reside in the United States or concerning any matter which is material and relevant to the enforcement of [the INA] and the administration of [DHS]''; Section 287(b) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1357(b), which authorizes the taking and consideration of evidence ``concerning any matter which is material or relevant to the enforcement of [the INA] and the administration of [DHS]''; Section 402 of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 202, which charges the Secretary with ``[e]stablishing and administering rules . . . governing the granting of visas or other forms of permission . . . to enter the United States'' and ``[e]stablishing national immigration enforcement policies and priorities''; see also HSA sec. 428, 6 U.S.C. 236; and Section 102(e) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 112(e), provides that ``the issuance of regulations by the Secretary shall be governed by the provisions of chapter 5 of title 5, except as specifically provided in this chapter, in laws granting regulatory authorities that are transferred by this chapter, and in laws enacted after November 25, 2002.''

Section 451(a)(3) and (b) of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 271(a)(3) and (b), transferring to USCIS the authority to adjudicate petitions for nonimmigrant status, establish policies for performing that function, and set national immigration services policies and priorities.

C. Extensions of Stay and Petition Validity

The petitioner must file Form I-129 to request an extension of stay for E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H-1B1, H-2A, H-2B, H-3, L-1, O-1, O-2, P-1, P-2, P-3, P-1S, P-2S, P-3S, Q-1, R-1, or TN nonimmigrant workers. For dependents of such workers, extension of stay requests may be filed on Form I-539, Application to Extend/Change Nonimmigrant Status.

Despite these well-established principles, the regulation at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 involving the same parties and the same underlying facts unless the officer determines that there was a material error involved with a prior approval, a material change in circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new, material information that adversely impacts eligibility. As discussed in Section III. of this preamble, DHS believes that the deference regulation is in tension with the statutory requirement that the petitioner must bear the burden to demonstrate eligibility for an immigration benefit, and it may unduly limit adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority in certain cases.

D. History of Deference in USCIS Adjudications

While the codification of deference was relatively recent, USCIS has had a history of implementing and rescinding deference through a series of policy actions beginning in 2004. First, in April 2004, USCIS issued a memorandum discussing the significance of prior USCIS adjudications. See USCIS, ``The Significance of a Prior CIS Approval of a Nonimmigrant Petition in the Context of a Subsequent Determination Regarding Eligibility for Extension of Petition Validity,'' HQPRD 72/11.3 (Apr. 23, 2004). This memorandum, while recognizing USCIS' authority to question prior determinations and that each matter must be decided according to the evidence of record on a case-by-case basis, first set out the policy instructing adjudications officers to give deference to a prior determination of eligibility in matters relating to an extension of nonimmigrant petition validity involving the same parties (petitioner and beneficiary) and the same underlying facts, unless there was material error, a substantial change in circumstances, or new material information. In October 2017, USCIS issued a memorandum which rescinded the 2004 guidance, expressing concerns that the 2004 memorandum improperly shifted the burden from the petitioner to USCIS. See USCIS, ``Rescission of Guidance Regarding Deference to Prior Determinations of Eligibility in the Adjudication of Petitions for Extension of Nonimmigrant Status,'' PM-602-0151 (Oct. 23, 2017). In the 2017 memorandum, USCIS also expressed concerns that the deference policy unduly limited adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority in certain cases. In April 2021, USCIS reinstituted its deference policy and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual. See USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 2, Part A, Chapter 4 ``Extension of Stay, Change of Status, and Extension of Petition Validity.'' The policy manual acknowledges that officers are not required to approve subsequent petitions where eligibility has not been demonstrated strictly because of a prior approval but stressed that they should defer to prior determinations involving the same parties and underlying facts. According to the policy manual, if an officer determines that deference to a prior approval is not appropriate, the officer must acknowledge the previous approval(s) in the denial, Request for Evidence (RFE), or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) and articulate the reason for not deferring to the previous determination (for example, due to a material error, change in circumstances, or new adverse material information). See id. Officers must provide the petitioner with an opportunity to respond to the new information consistent with 8 CFR 103.2(b)(16)(i). See id. In December 2024, DHS codified its deference policy at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) through the final rule Modernizing H-1B Requirements, Providing Flexibility in the F-1 Program, and Program Improvements Affecting Other Nonimmigrant Workers, 89 FR 103054 (Dec. 18, 2024) (Modernization Final Rule). Current 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) states that when adjudicating a Form I-129, Petition for Nonimmigrant Worker, involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, USCIS gives deference to its prior determination of eligibility unless there is a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility.

III. Discussion of Proposed Rule

DHS proposes to remove its regulation at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), and the deference policy, which instructs USCIS officers to give deference to a prior determination of the petitioner's or beneficiary's eligibility when adjudicating a request filed on Form I-129 involving the same parties and the same underlying facts, unless there was a material error, a material change, or new material information that adversely impacts eligibility. This proposed change would apply to all benefit requests filed using Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker. This proposal would not prohibit USCIS officers from considering a prior approval where relevant. Rather, it would remove the requirement that officers begin from a position of deference to the prior approval. DHS believes that this change would better ensure that officers fully consider all relevant facts and evidence to ensure continued eligibility, and adjudicate each petition or request on a case-by-case basis to determine whether the petitioner has met its burden of proof to demonstrate continued eligibility for the benefit. Overall, DHS believes that removing deference would enhance program integrity and thereby better protect the interests of U.S. workers, consistent with this Administration's priorities.

A. Restoring the Proper Allocation of the Burden of Proof

Removing deference would better align DHS regulations with the agency's longstanding interpretation of section 291 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1361, which places the burden of proof on the petitioner or applicant to establish eligibility for each immigration benefit sought. See also Matter of Chawathe, 25 I. & N. Dec. 369, 375 n.7 (USCIS AAO, 2010) (``The burden of proving eligibility for the benefit sought remains entirely with the applicant.''). Although an agency may establish reasonable evidentiary presumptions, see e.g., Reno v. Flores, 507 U.S. 292, 313 (1993), any such presumption must be consistent with the statutory text and scheme, see Lin v. U.S. Dep't of Justice, 494 F.3d 296, 308 (2d Cir. 2007) (en banc). Whether or not the deference regulation is consonant with the statute, DHS now believes that it has the practical effect of shifting the burden of proof from the petitioner to the agency, in tension with section 291 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1361, with respect to the eligibility criteria that Congress intended the agency to determine for each immigration benefit sought. When DHS promulgated 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), the agency stated that petitioners would continue to have the burden to demonstrate continued eligibility for the requested nonimmigrant worker classification. See 89 FR 103094. In practice, however, the deference policy effectively shifts the burden from the petitioner to the adjudicating officer who must identify a material error or change in circumstances to justify deviating from the prior approval. In effect, this creates a default position that the prior approval was correct, and the petitioner and beneficiary remain eligible for the benefit unless the officer finds that an enumerated exception to the deference policy applies (i.e., that there was a material error, material change in circumstances or eligibility requirements, or new, material information that adversely impacts eligibility). This structure effectively shifts the burden from the petitioner to the adjudicating officer. Instead of requiring the petitioner to establish that the alien is eligible to continue to work in the United States under a nonimmigration classification, the deference regulation and policy effectively require the officer to justify why the prior approval should not control.

B. Enhancing USCIS Officer Fact-Finding Authority

Removing deference would also better ensure that USCIS officers review the facts and evidence in every case to ensure continued eligibility before approving a petition extension and granting an extension of stay request. The deference policy suggests that a less than thorough review of each case may be acceptable and gives the impression of unduly limiting adjudicating officers' inherent fact-finding authority. Some officers may view deference as a restriction on their ability to consider all the facts of the case. Rather than taking appropriate action if eligibility was not demonstrated in the petition (such as issuing an RFE), some officers may simply grant the benefit absent glaring errors or changes as a result of the deference policy. Indeed, as shown in Table 3 infra, the RFE rate increased by 2.9 percent more than the RFE rate for the comparison group after the deference policy was rescinded in 2017. DHS acknowledges that other changes unrelated to deference may have, in part, contributed to this increased RFE rate. However, DHS believes that it is reasonable to conclude that the rescission of the deference policy was one of the contributing factors for this increased RFE rate. This increase is consistent with DHS's concern that the deference policy has had the effect of discouraging some officers from requesting additional evidence even in cases where the petitioner has not established eligibility for the nonimmigrant worker classification in connection with the current request. An adjudicating officer's fact-finding authority should not be constrained by any prior petition approval. Instead, officers should thoroughly review a petition for eligibility and request additional documentation as appropriate based on the merits of each case, consistent with USCIS policy regarding requests for evidence, notices of intent to deny, and the adjudication of petitions for nonimmigrant benefits. Because deference may be viewed as a default position upon beginning review of certain filings, the deference policy may, in some cases, have had the unintended effect of limiting the ability of officers to conduct a thorough review of the facts and limiting assessment of eligibility in each case. While officers may, of course, reach the same conclusion as in a prior decision, they should not be compelled to do so as a default starting point. DHS data also show that historical denial rates did not statistically differ during periods when the deference policy was in effect compared to when it was not in effect. One possible reason for this is that even when deference did not apply, petitioners may have been able to overcome issues raised in an RFE or NOID by submitting additional evidence or information. DHS believes, however, that the impact of the deference policy on officers' fact-finding authority is best reflected in RFE rates rather than approval or denial rates. The ultimate adjudicative decision reached by the officer is not reflective of the extent to which an officer's fact-finding authority may have been restricted during the adjudicative review process. Rather, the variations in RFE rates during periods when deference applied versus the RFE rate when deference did not apply strongly suggests that deference has had the effect of discouraging some officers from requesting additional evidence. Policies that discourage officers from issuing RFEs, even when the officer determines that the petitioner has not yet established eligibility, undermine the integrity of the lawful immigration system and are inconsistent with enhancing an officer's fact-finding authority, regardless of the ultimate adjudicative decision.

In addition, deference increases the risk of officers not discovering material errors in prior adjudications. Although the deference policy allows officers to deviate from the prior decision if there was a material error, if officers limited their review of the cases before them because of an assumption that the prior decision was correct, it would necessarily limit the discovery of material error. Deferring to a determination of eligibility for nonimmigrant worker classification that was made potentially up to several years before the adjudication of the petition extension, and that may be based on inaccurate or outdated facts or adjudicated under regulations which have changed since the original approval was issued, is inconsistent with this Administration's efforts to strengthen the integrity of the nonimmigrant worker system. USCIS does not believe additional officer training or clarification on how to apply deference would sufficiently address these concerns. As discussed earlier in this preamble, USCIS has a history of applying deference over several years. Prior to its codification in the regulations in 2024, the deference policy was in place at USCIS from 2004 until its rescission in 2017 and was reinstituted in 2021. Therefore, USCIS officers generally have had training and operational guidance on how to adjudicate petitions with the deference policy in place. Training, however, is not the issue or solution. Rather, any deference requirement itself conveys a fundamental tension with an officer's obligation to conduct a fulsome review to ensure that the petitioner met its burden before granting a nonimmigrant worker benefit. Indeed, the deference policy was based in part on a desire to increase efficiency by reducing the officer's need to revisit prior determinations of eligibility. That efficiency, however, has had the unintended effect of discouraging officers from thoroughly reviewing a case when adjudicating extension requests for nonimmigrant worker classifications. DHS now believes that the deference policy is inconsistent with ensuring that officers fully evaluate eligibility in every case, which is necessary to protect the integrity of the immigration benefits system and the interests of U.S. workers by ensuring that petitioners and beneficiaries are eligible for the requested nonimmigrant worker benefit.

C. Strengthening Program Integrity

DHS also believes that deference may undermine program integrity, including by creating opportunities for unscrupulous petitioners to submit fraudulent or misleading petitions for nonimmigrant worker benefits. For example, an unscrupulous filer might submit a petition of questionable merit, hoping that if it is approved, the approval can be used as an anchor for later filings involving similar facts, related beneficiaries, or the same employer. They may even file multiple of these types of petitions and use the fact pattern that is the most advantageous or that is the most quickly approved. Similarly, a petitioner might overstate the beneficiary's role, compensation, or qualifications in the first filing, expecting that once approved, future filings will receive less scrutiny. Further, petitioners may be less forthcoming about changes affecting their business operations or the proffered position (such as reduced operations, loss of contracts, altered job duties, or other compliance issues) if they believe a prior approval is binding. If deference is expected, the petitioner may be incentivized to file extensions without fully disclosing those changes. Indeed, USCIS data provides some support for the concern that deference may undermine program integrity by reducing scrutiny in some cases and contributing to an environment in which misleading, non-compliant, or fraudulent extensions of nonimmigrant worker petitions are more likely to be approved. For example, the data demonstrate higher percentages of fraud and non-compliance identified in the H-1B and L-1A programs since the time when USCIS reinstituted its deference policy and incorporated it into the USCIS Policy Manual. Specifically, for H-1B extension cases from FY 2022 through FY 2025, the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among H-1B sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits was 22.39 percent. In comparison, when USCIS had a policy of no deference, the overall combined percentage of H-1B non-compliance and/ or fraud among H-1B sites visited during FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 16.77 percent. For L-1A extension cases, the overall combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited during USCIS administrative and targeted site visits from FY 2022 through FY 2025 was 24.46 percent. In comparison, the overall combined percentage of L-1A non-compliance and/or fraud among L-1A sites visited from FY 2018 through FY 2020 was 18.37 percent. USCIS, Releasable Data Regarding Fraud and Noncompliance in the H-1B and L-1A Programs (Jun. 6, 2026). This data represents administrative and targeted site visits conducted exclusively on H-1B and L-1A extension petitions. USCIS excluded FY 2021 data from this subset because the deference policy was reinstated partway through FY 2021 (in April 2021) and was not in effect for more than half of that fiscal year. USCIS excluded FY 2021 data from this subset because the deference policy was reinstated partway through FY 2021 (in April 2021) and was not in effect for more than half of that fiscal year.

In other words, during the years that USCIS had a policy of deference, the combined percentage of non-compliance and/or fraud among sites visited in the H-1B and L-1A programs was higher than in the years that USCIS did not have a policy of deference. This trend reflected in a subset of H-1B and L-1A extension filings supports the concern that deference undermines program integrity in potentially limiting USCIS' ability to thoroughly review an extension petition on a case-by-case basis, which in turn may incentivize frivolous or fraudulent filings that falsely assert no material change. While DHS acknowledges that other factors besides or in addition to deference may have led to this higher percentage of identifying fraud or non-compliance, it is reasonable to conclude that deference was one of the contributing factors. Removing deference would potentially disincentivize fraudulent filings and help restore the integrity of the lawful immigration system. This, in turn, would also better protect U.S. workers by ensuring that petitions for nonimmigrant workers are only approved if eligibility is established by the petitioner based on evidence submitted in support of each petition.

D. Reconsideration of the Deference Policy

DHS acknowledges the history of the deference policy and its recent codification at 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5) in the Modernization Final Rule. DHS also acknowledges that some of the statements in this proposed rule represent a shift from statements made in the Modernization Final Rule. In the Modernization Final Rule, some commenters voiced concern that codifying deference would constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding authority. See 89 FR 103093. Commenters stated that USCIS officers should not be constrained in requesting additional evidence in the adjudication process. They also stated that requiring USCIS officers to confirm all material facts before granting a benefit request would serve as a fraud detection mechanism and deterrent. At the time, DHS disagreed with the commenters' concerns. Id. However, DHS has reconsidered the issue since publication of the Modernization Final Rule and now believes that codification of the deference policy may have had the unintended effect of appearing to constrain USCIS officers' fact-finding authority, leading some USCIS officers to conduct a less than fulsome review, and thus undermining the agency's efforts to detect and deter fraud. See FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009) (``[I]t suffices that the new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are good reasons for it, and that the agency believes it to be better, which the conscious change of course adequately indicates.'').

Removing 30-Day Refugee Termination Notice

AGENCY: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

ACTION: Interim final rule.

SUMMARY: This interim final rule (IFR) amends Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations to expedite termination of refugee status when DHS determines an alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time of admission to the United States. The response period to a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) is reduced from thirty to ten days. These changes aim to restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and exploitation.

II. Executive Summary

A. Purpose of the Regulatory Action

The purpose of this rulemaking is to shorten the termination notice period in order to mitigate potential risks posed by aliens admitted to the United States as refugees when, in fact, they were not eligible for refugee classification at the time of admission. Those who are improperly admitted may not have their identity fully confirmed and vetted due to an incomplete record, and as such pose a risk to program integrity and may pose a risk to national security and public safety. A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records. Operational guidance implemented during this period allowed officers to forgo typical lines of inquiry, sacrificing the caliber and efficacy of the refugee interview, a critical screening component of the refugee adjudication process. The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews. Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States. This is supported by a recent preliminary review of admitted refugees residing in Minnesota who were interviewed, approved, and admitted during the Biden administration. For the majority of these reviewed cases, the evidence was insufficient to establish that the principal applicant met all of the required elements of the refugee definition. The goal was to have as many refugees as practicable enter the United States to meet President Biden's ceiling for refugee admissions and in order to accomplish this, a number of requirements for ensuring a thorough examination and assessment of eligibility were reduced or removed.

This raises concerns about the integrity of the refugee program and calls into question the eligibility for refugee status of aliens admitted to the United States during this time. As detailed below in this preamble, several policy decisions were implemented that significantly reduced the integrity measures within the refugee program. These changes resulted in an increase in the number of refugee interviews conducted per officer each day, with less comprehensive elicitation of testimony from applicants. These adjustments limited the ability of refugee officers, and the U.S. government to accurately determine whether an applicant's identity was properly established, assess potential national security or public safety concerns, and verify whether the applicant met the definition of a refugee. To protect U.S. interests and public safety, USCIS must act swiftly when DHS determines that an alien did not meet the refugee definition and was not entitled to refugee status at the time of admission. Shortening the NOIT response period enables DHS to respond rapidly to such findings. Allowing a longer notice period could provide opportunities for aliens to evade enforcement or engage in harmful activities. For example, the Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) Directorate investigated cases where refugees were later identified as members of armed groups or had concealed extremist affiliations. In one case, a refugee was found to have participated in human rights abuses with the Liberian Armed Forces during the Liberian Civil War. In another case, a refugee was found to have misrepresented his involvement with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), an armed group in Ethiopia. Social media checks indicated numerous pro-OLF activities and pro-OLF and radical violent rhetoric posted prior to his admission to the United States as a refugee. These cases demonstrate that when credible evidence of national security or public safety concerns arises after a refugee's admission, USCIS may be unable to initiate removal proceedings until the termination process is complete. Therefore, reducing the response period to ten days after issuance of a NOIT allows USCIS to address such threats more quickly and effectively, restoring integrity to the immigration system. To be eligible for admission to the United States as a refugee, an alien must establish, among other things, that they meet the definition of ``refugee'' as defined in section 101(a)(42)(A) and (B) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) and (B), which includes the requirement that they are not a persecutor. When USCIS discovers after an alien's admission to the United States that they should not have been admitted because they did not meet the refugee definition and therefore the eligibility requirements for refugee classification at the time of admission, it is important to protect the integrity of the American immigration system by taking whatever steps are legally available, including ensuring that the alien is removed from the United States as quickly as possible where there is a legal basis to do so. There is an inherent risk to national security and public safety when an alien's identity has not been fully established. Therefore, the ability to streamline refugee status termination, where appropriate, contributes immediately to the safety of the American people and the integrity of the lawful U.S. immigration system. The current notice and response process for terminating refugee status upon determination that the alien was not a refugee at the time of their admission is inefficient and compromises the security and safety of the United States. Providing 30 days to respond to a NOIT, instead of a 10-day response period, allows ineligible aliens more time to retain immigration benefits to which they are not entitled, undermining the integrity of the U.S. immigration system and national interests of the United States. Moreover, when an alien retains a status he or she is not entitled to, while also being inadequately vetted with insufficient information as to their true identity, there is a risk to American society's safety and security.

C. Summary of the Regulatory Action

Through this IFR, DHS is amending 8 CFR 207.9 to change the 30-day notice-and-response period for aliens whose refugee status is terminated by USCIS to a 10-day notice-and-response period.

D. Related Rulemakings

III. Background and Purpose

A. Initial Refugee Processing

Refugee status in the United States is a highly sought after immigration benefit for displaced persons throughout the world due in part to the benefits it bestows as well as a pathway to permanent status. Resettlement to the United States through the United States Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) is a multi-step process involving several agency partners. The U.S. Department of State (State) leads the annual consultations process, funds and oversees refugee resettlement activities, contracts with the non-governmental organizations that provide pre- and post-USCIS interview support, and facilitates the Priority 1 referrals to the USRAP process. After an alien is determined to have access to the USRAP, they may file a Form I-590, Registration for Classification as Refugee. Applications for refugee classification are primarily processed overseas and adjudicated by USCIS Refugee Officers who determine whether an alien meets the refugee definition and is otherwise eligible for resettlement to the United States. Under United States law, to be eligible for refugee classification an applicant must establish that he or she:

8 CFR 207.4 (authority for CBP to admit aliens approved for refugee classification).

Derivatives of the principal refugee applicant may include the spouse of a principal refugee and their unmarried children under the age of 21. Derivative family members may be included in the initial application for refugee status or petitioned for after the principal refugee's arrival to the United States. Id. For derivatives to be admitted to the United States as refugees, they must establish that they are admissible and not subject to the persecutor bar but are not required to prove that they meet the refugee definition or any of its elements, such as past persecution or a well-founded fear of future persecution.

INA 207(c)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(2).

In addition to resettlement in the United States, refugees receive employment authorization as soon as they arrive in the United States. 8 CFR 274a.12(a)(3).

B. Termination of Refugee Status

The sole basis for USCIS to terminate the status of an alien conditionally admitted to the United States as a refugee is if USCIS determines that the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of admission to the United States. No other ground of termination is specified under the law. An alien who did not, in fact, meet the refugee definition at the time of admission would have been inadmissible, and once that status is terminated, will generally lack legal grounds to remain in the United States. INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4). See 8 CFR. 207.9 (permitting termination of refugee status only if USCIS determines the alien ``was not a refugee'' within the meaning of INA section 101(a)(42) at the time of admission); INA section 237(a)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(1)(A) (making deportable any noncitizen who was inadmissible ``at the time of entry''), incorporating, inter alia, INA section 212(a)(7)(A)(i)(I), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(7)(A)(i)(I) (inadmissibility for lack of valid immigrant entry document).

The determination to terminate refugee status because the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of his or her admission to the United States applies solely to principal refugees and not to derivative refugees. In order to be eligible for refugee status, principal applicants must meet the requirements of the refugee definition in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), must be admissible to the United States, and must qualify under one of the designated USRAP processing priorities. USCIS may in turn terminate a derivative refugee's status if the principal's status is terminated. INA 291, 207(c)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1361, 1157(c)(1). See 8 CFR 207.7(d) and 207.9, see also INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4) providing that the ``refugee status of any alien (and of the spouse or child of the alien), may be terminated'' (emphasis added).

When USCIS determines that a principal refugee was not a refugee as defined in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), at the time of admission, USCIS initiates termination of refugee status. The former Immigration and Naturalization Service first implemented regulations governing the termination of refugee status following the enactment of the Refugee Act of 1980, and the process has remained substantively unchanged in the 45 years since then. 45 FR 37392 (June 2, 1980) (interim final rule); 46 FR 45116 (Sept. 10, 1981) (final rule). INS and DHS have made only minimal changes to 8 CFR 207.9 since it was first published. Following the enactment of IIRIRA, INS updated the references to the types of removal proceedings that may apply following a termination of refugee status. See also, Inspection and Expedited Removal of Aliens; Detention and Removal of Aliens; Conduct of Removal Proceedings; Asylum Procedures, 62 FR 10312, 10337 (Mar. 6, 1997). Other minor changes included renumbering from 207.8 to 207.9 and including updated DHS service procedures. Procedures for Filing a Derivative Petition (Form I-730) for a Spouse and Unmarried Children of a Refugee/Asylee, 63 FR 3792 (Jan. 27, 1998); Immigration Benefits Business Transformation, Increment I, 76 FR 53764, 53784 (Aug. 29, 2011).

USCIS issues a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) prior to termination. In the NOIT, USCIS outlines the specific basis or bases for the termination, such as a determination by USCIS that the harm the alien experienced or feared was not on account of a protected ground or, for example, that the alien had another nationality or legal status in another country such that they did not qualify as a refugee from the claimed country. The NOIT further informs the alien of his or her right to offer written or oral evidence in support of his or her refugee claim and in opposition to the proposed termination. Prior to this IFR, 8 CFR 207.9 provided that the alien has a 30-day period to respond to a NOIT. The preamble implementing this process did not explain the Immigration and Nationality Service's (INS) reasoning for the 30-day response period (as opposed to some other shorter or longer period). \22 \ 8 CFR 207.9. \23 \ 45 FR 37392; 46 FR 45116.

If the alien chooses to provide oral testimony, he or she must notify USCIS of his or her request for an additional interview so that USCIS may schedule the interview within 30 days of the date of the notice. The alien may also submit documentary evidence within 30 days from the date of the notice to the return address that is listed at the top of the notice. The NOIT makes clear that lack of a response to the notice within the time allotted results in termination of the alien's refugee status.

Finally, the NOIT states that if USCIS determines that the alien was not a refugee within the meaning of section 101(a)(42) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), at the time of admission, his or her refugee status and employment authorization will be terminated, and he or she will be subject to removal from the United States. DHS typically reviews an alien's underlying refugee determination prior to the final adjudication of his or her adjustment of status to permanent residence and initiates termination when warranted. However, termination may be initiated at any time prior to adjustment if DHS determines the alien was not eligible for refugee status at the time he or she was admitted as a refugee. There is no appeal from the termination of refugee status by USCIS. Upon termination USCIS processes the alien for removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA. Id. Id.

USCIS may also place a person who was admitted as a refugee directly in removal proceedings, without termination of refugee status, on the basis of any applicable removal charge without the adjudication of an adjustment application. See Matter of Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836, 838 (BIA 2005) (explaining that ``Congress did not consider termination of refugee status to be a prerequisite to initiating removal proceedings against aliens admitted as refugees.'').

C. Actions by the Prior Administration That Increased the Risk of Errant Refugee Admissions

Each year, the president sets the refugee ceiling, created by the Refugee Act of 1980. INA 207(a)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(a)(2). During President Trump's first term he reduced the number each fiscal year (FY) (and additionally COVID-19 drastically reduced actual admissions) in order to review the program's integrity and make sure proper screening and vetting measures were in place and in order to shift resources to deal with the crisis at the U.S. southern border. Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2018, 82 FR 49083 (Oct. 23, 2017); Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2019, 83 FR 55091 (Nov. 1, 2018); Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2020, 84 FR 65903 (Nov. 29, 2019); Presidential Determination on Refugee Admissions for Fiscal Year 2021, 85 FR 71219 (Nov. 6, 2020).

During the following Biden administration; however, the Presidential Determination increased to a high not seen since the late 80s and early 90s. The refugee admission cap was repeatedly set at 125,000 from FY 2022 through FY 2025. Refugee actual admissions under the Biden administration reached its peak in FY 2024, which was 100,034 admissions--the highest in three decades. In order to reach this historically high level of refugee admissions, as evidenced by a number of updated policies and procedures, USCIS prioritized speed of processing over properly screening aliens. These changes to processing included, but were not limited to:

The majority of these changes impacted the quality of the refugee interview required under regulation. The main reasons officers elicit information during an interview are to: verify the identity of those present at the interview; determine whether to proceed with the interview; determine eligibility for a benefit being sought (if the interview relates to an application for a benefit); determine whether the individual being interviewed is subject to any bars or grounds of inadmissibility; evaluate the credibility; and identify whether fraud may be involved. Accordingly, the refugee interview is an instrumental component of robustly screening a refugee applicant. More truncated, less thorough interviews under the Biden administration damaged the integrity of refugee processing by hindering the officers' ability to appropriately gather sufficient information related to the aforementioned purposes of the refugee interview and to make an appropriate and legally sufficient decision. Consequently, these changes enabled ineligible aliens to exploit the refugee program to resettle in the United States, where they then have a path to permanent status, including citizenship.
